about: ELEC0002 is the core first-year electronic engineering module taught in Term 1 at UCL (15 credits). According to the 2026/27 module catalogue it covers energy sources and heat-engine efficiency, DC and AC circuit analysis, filters and resonance, three-phase systems, binary arithmetic and combinational logic, microcontroller programming (for example the Arduino Uno), op-amps and single-loop feedback control, alongside practical work with test instruments and circuit building. It is taught in person and assessed 70% by exam and 30% by coursework (2026/27 catalogue).
topics: Energy, power and heat-engine efficiency (Carnot and endoreversible)
Kirchhoff's laws, circuit analysis, Thévenin and Norton equivalents
Capacitance, inductance, impedance and maximum power transfer
Phasors and complex algebra in circuit analysis
Binary numbers, binary arithmetic and Boolean algebra
Operational amplifiers: amplifiers, integrators and differentiators

notes.h: Energy, power and the limits on heat engines
notes.body:
The module opens by placing electronic and electrical engineering inside the bigger energy picture: where electrical energy comes from, how much of the fuel's energy actually ends up as electricity, and why there is a hard thermodynamic ceiling on that fraction.

Force, energy and power
- Work done by a force: W = F × d (for a force along the direction of motion). Units: joules (J = N m).
- Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = dE/dt. For a force moving at speed v, P = F v. Units: watts (W = J/s).
- Electrical power: P = V I; for a resistor P = I²R = V²/R.
- Energy billing uses the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 MJ. A 2 kW kettle running for 3 minutes uses 2000 × 180 = 360 kJ = 0.1 kWh.

Energy sources and fuel types
- Chemical fuels (coal, oil products, natural gas, biomass) release energy by combustion; nuclear fuel by fission; renewables (wind, solar, hydro) convert a natural flow directly.
- Rough specific energies (approximate, for comparison only): natural gas about 50–55 MJ/kg, petrol about 45 MJ/kg, coal about 24–30 MJ/kg, a lithium-ion cell only about 0.5–0.9 MJ/kg. This gap is why batteries struggle to replace liquid fuels where mass matters.
- Thermal power stations (coal, gas, nuclear) all use a heat engine, so they are bound by the limits below. Wind, hydro and photovoltaics are not heat engines and are not limited by the Carnot formula.

Carnot efficiency
A heat engine takes heat Q_h from a hot reservoir at absolute temperature T_h, rejects Q_c to a cold reservoir at T_c and delivers work W = Q_h − Q_c. Efficiency η = W/Q_h. The second law of thermodynamics limits any engine running between two reservoirs to
- η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h, with both temperatures in kelvin.
Example: T_h = 800 K, T_c = 300 K gives η = 1 − 300/800 = 0.625 (62.5 %). Using degrees Celsius instead of kelvin is the classic error and gives nonsense.

Endoreversible (Curzon–Ahlborn) efficiency
A Carnot engine is reversible, so it must run infinitely slowly and delivers zero power. A more realistic model keeps the internal cycle reversible but lets heat flow into and out of it through finite thermal resistances. Maximising the output power of this "endoreversible" engine gives the efficiency at maximum power:
- η_CA = 1 − √(T_c/T_h).
For 800 K and 300 K: η_CA = 1 − √0.375 ≈ 0.388 (38.8 %), much closer to what real plants achieve than the Carnot figure. The engine trades efficiency for power: running closer to Carnot efficiency means delivering less power.

Key points
- Always convert to kelvin (K = °C + 273.15).
- η_CA < η_Carnot for any T_c < T_h.
- Raising T_h (better materials) or lowering T_c raises both limits.

Exam tips: state which efficiency you are quoting (maximum possible vs efficiency at maximum power), show the kelvin conversion, and sanity-check that the answer lies between 0 and 1.

Almost every circuit problem in the module comes down to applying two conservation laws and Ohm's law systematically.

The laws
- Ohm's law: V = I R for a linear resistor.
- Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the algebraic sum of currents leaving any node is zero (conservation of charge).
- Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (conservation of energy, a consequence of the potential being single-valued).
- Series resistors add: R = R₁ + R₂. Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, so two in parallel give R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
- Voltage divider: V_out = V_in R₂/(R₁ + R₂) (unloaded). Current divider: I₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂).

Systematic methods
- Nodal analysis: choose a reference node, write KCL at every other node with node voltages as unknowns. Best when there are few nodes.
- Mesh analysis: assign a current to each independent loop and write KVL. Best when there are few meshes.
- Superposition (linear circuits only): find the response to each independent source alone, with other voltage sources replaced by short circuits and current sources by open circuits, then add. It works for voltages and currents, not for power.

Thévenin and Norton
Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, as seen from its terminals, by:
- Thévenin: a voltage source V_Th in series with R_Th.
- Norton: a current source I_N in parallel with R_N.
- V_Th = open-circuit voltage; I_N = short-circuit current; R_Th = R_N = V_Th/I_N. With only independent sources, R_Th can also be found by turning off the sources and finding the resistance seen at the terminals.

Worked example
A 12 V source in series with R₁ = 4 kΩ feeds a node; R₂ = 12 kΩ connects that node to ground; the output is taken across R₂.
- V_Th = 12 × 12/(4 + 12) = 9 V.
- R_Th = 4 kΩ ∥ 12 kΩ = 48/16 = 3 kΩ.
- I_N = 9 V/3 kΩ = 3 mA (check: shorting the output gives 12 V/4 kΩ = 3 mA).
- With a 6 kΩ load: I = 9/(3 + 6) kΩ = 1 mA and V_load = 6 V, much less than the 9 V open-circuit value. This "loading" effect is why the equivalent is useful.

Sign conventions
Use the passive sign convention: if current enters the + terminal of an element, the power absorbed is P = V I. A negative result means the element is delivering power.

Exam tips: draw and label node voltages before writing equations; check R_Th two ways (source-off and V_oc/I_sc); remember superposition does not apply to power.

notes.h: Capacitors, inductors, impedance and maximum power transfer
notes.body:
Capacitors and inductors store energy rather than dissipate it, and their behaviour depends on how fast signals change. Impedance extends Ohm's law to them for sinusoidal signals.

Capacitance
- Definition: Q = C V; unit farad (F). Parallel-plate capacitor: C = ε₀ε_r A/d.
- Current–voltage law: i = C dv/dt. A capacitor's voltage cannot change instantaneously (that would need infinite current).
- Stored energy: E = ½ C V². Example: 100 µF at 10 V stores 5 mJ.
- In DC steady state a capacitor carries no current: it acts as an open circuit.
- Capacitors add in parallel (C = C₁ + C₂) and combine like resistors in parallel when in series.

Inductance
- v = L di/dt; unit henry (H). An inductor's current cannot change instantaneously, which is why switching off an inductive load produces a large voltage spike (hence flyback diodes across relay coils).
- Stored energy: E = ½ L I². Example: 10 mH carrying 2 A stores 20 mJ.
- In DC steady state an inductor is a short circuit.

First-order transients
For an RC circuit charged from a step V through R: v_C(t) = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with τ = RC. After one τ the capacitor reaches about 63 % of its final value; after 5τ about 99.3 %. For RL circuits τ = L/R.

Impedance
For sinusoidal steady state at angular frequency ω = 2πf, with the convention that d/dt becomes multiplication by jω:
- Resistor: Z_R = R.
- Inductor: Z_L = jωL (impedance rises with frequency; current lags voltage by 90°).
- Capacitor: Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) (impedance falls with frequency; current leads voltage by 90°).
- Example: 1 µF at 1 kHz has |Z| = 1/(2π × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 159 Ω.
Impedances combine exactly like resistances (series add, parallel by product over sum), using complex arithmetic.

Maximum power transfer
For a source with Thévenin resistance R_Th, a resistive load receives the most power when R_L = R_Th, and then
- P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th).
- Example: V_Th = 9 V, R_Th = 3 kΩ gives P_max = 81/12000 = 6.75 mW.
- At this point the efficiency is only 50 %: as much power is lost in R_Th as reaches the load. Power systems are therefore designed for high efficiency (R_L ≫ R_source), while communications and sensor front-ends are often matched for maximum power.
For AC with source impedance Z_Th = R_Th + jX_Th, the load that takes maximum power is the complex conjugate Z_L = R_Th − jX_Th, which cancels the reactance; with an rms phasor V_Th the power is then |V_Th|²/(4R_Th).

Exam tips: treat C as open and L as short for DC steady state; quote units (µF, mH) carefully; remember matching gives maximum power, not maximum efficiency.

Phasors turn differential equations for sinusoidal steady state into ordinary algebra with complex numbers. They only apply when every source in the circuit is a sinusoid of the same frequency and transients have died away.

Complex numbers refresher
- Rectangular form: z = a + jb (engineers use j because i is current). Polar form: z = r∠θ with r = √(a² + b²), θ = atan2(b, a).
- Euler's formula: e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, so r∠θ = r e^(jθ).
- Add and subtract in rectangular form; multiply and divide in polar form (multiply magnitudes, add angles; divide magnitudes, subtract angles).
- 1/j = −j, and j × j = −1. Multiplying by j rotates a phasor by +90°.
- Watch the quadrant when computing angles: −1 − j has angle −135°, not +45°.

The phasor idea
- A sinusoid v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ) is represented by the phasor V = V_m∠φ (convention used here: cosine reference). Many power texts use rms magnitudes instead, V = (V_m/√2)∠φ; state which you use.
- v(t) = Re{V e^(jωt)}. Differentiating multiplies by jω, integrating divides by jω, which is where Z_L = jωL and Z_C = 1/(jωC) come from.
- KCL, KVL, Ohm's law (V = Z I), dividers, nodal/mesh analysis and Thévenin all work unchanged with phasors and impedances.

Worked example
A 10 V rms, ω = 2000 rad/s source drives R = 100 Ω in series with L = 50 mH.
- X_L = ωL = 2000 × 0.05 = 100 Ω, so Z = 100 + j100 = 141.4∠45° Ω.
- I = V/Z = 10∠0°/141.4∠45° = 0.0707∠−45° A rms: the current lags the voltage by 45°.
- Real power P = I²R = 0.0707² × 100 = 0.5 W. Apparent power |S| = V I = 0.707 VA. Power factor cos 45° ≈ 0.707 (lagging).

AC power with rms phasors
- Complex power S = V I* = P + jQ, where I* is the complex conjugate.
- P (watts) is average power; Q (volt-amperes reactive, var) is the energy shuttling back and forth in L and C; |S| (VA) is apparent power.
- Power factor = P/|S| = cos φ, where φ is the angle by which voltage leads current. Inductive loads have lagging power factor (Q > 0).
- If peak-value phasors are used instead, P = ½ V_m I_m cos φ; mixing the two conventions is a common source of factor-of-two errors.

Phasor diagrams
Draw V and I as arrows in the complex plane. For a series RL circuit, V_R is in phase with I, V_L leads I by 90°, and V = V_R + V_L forms a right-angled triangle.

Exam tips: state your convention (peak or rms, cosine reference) at the start; convert to rectangular for addition; check the angle sign tells you whether the circuit is inductive (current lags) or capacitive (current leads).

Because capacitor and inductor impedances depend on frequency, simple RC, RL and RLC networks pass some frequencies and reject others. These are the first filters met in the course.

Transfer function and decibels
- The frequency response H(jω) = V_out/V_in (phasors). Its magnitude is the gain and its angle the phase shift.
- Gain in decibels: 20 log₁₀|H| for voltage ratios (10 log₁₀ for power ratios). A factor of 1/√2 in voltage is −3.01 dB, i.e. half power.

First-order RC low-pass (output across C)
- H = Z_C/(R + Z_C) = 1/(1 + jωRC).
- Cut-off (corner) frequency: ω_c = 1/(RC), f_c = 1/(2πRC). There |H| = 1/√2 (−3 dB) and the phase is −45°.
- Well above f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade (6 dB per octave) and the phase tends to −90°.
- Example: R = 1 kΩ, C = 100 nF gives f_c = 1/(2π × 10³ × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 1.59 kHz. At 10 f_c the gain is about −20 dB.

First-order RC high-pass (output across R)
- H = jωRC/(1 + jωRC); same f_c, gain rises at 20 dB/decade below f_c, phase +45° at f_c.
- An RL network gives the same shapes with τ = L/R; output across L is high-pass, across R is low-pass.

Series RLC resonance
- Z = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC)). The reactances cancel at the resonant frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC), f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
- At resonance |Z| is a minimum (= R), the current is a maximum and in phase with the source.
- Quality factor Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C). The −3 dB bandwidth is B = f₀/Q = R/(2πL).
- At resonance the voltage across L (and across C) is Q times the source voltage, so a high-Q circuit can develop voltages much larger than the supply.

Worked example
L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF, R = 10 Ω.
- f₀ = 1/(2π√(10⁻² × 10⁻⁷)) = 1/(2π × 3.162 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 5.03 kHz.
- Q = (1/10)√(10⁻²/10⁻⁷) = √10⁵/10 ≈ 31.6.
- Bandwidth = 5033/31.6 ≈ 159 Hz (check: R/(2πL) = 10/(0.0628) ≈ 159 Hz).
- With a 1 V supply at resonance, V_L ≈ V_C ≈ 31.6 V.

Parallel RLC
For an ideal parallel LC with R in parallel, resonance is at the same ω₀ but the impedance is a maximum there (the L and C currents cancel), so the circuit rejects the source current at f₀; the Q for the parallel case is R√(C/L).

Uses
Band-pass filters for radio tuning, notch filters to reject mains hum, and simple low-pass filters to smooth PWM outputs from microcontrollers.

Exam tips: always state f_c or f₀ in hertz and ω in rad/s and do not mix them; quote −3 dB at cut-off; sketch Bode plots with straight-line asymptotes and label slopes.

Nearly all grid electricity is generated, transmitted and distributed as three-phase AC. This topic introduces balanced three-phase circuits and the machine that generates them.

Balanced three-phase supply
- Three sinusoidal voltages of equal magnitude, 120° apart: V_a = V∠0°, V_b = V∠−120°, V_c = V∠+120° (positive sequence a-b-c).
- In a balanced system the three voltages (and currents) sum to zero at every instant.
- Advantages: for a balanced load the total instantaneous power is constant (smooth torque in motors); less conductor material for the same power than single-phase; three-phase windings naturally produce a rotating magnetic field.

Star (Y) and delta (Δ) connections
- Star: line voltage V_L = √3 × phase voltage V_ph, and line current = phase current. A neutral can be provided.
- Delta: V_L = V_ph, and line current I_L = √3 × phase current.
- UK low-voltage supply is nominally 400 V line-to-line and 230 V line-to-neutral (400/√3 ≈ 231 V).
- Line voltages lead the corresponding phase voltages by 30° in a positive-sequence star system.

Three-phase power (balanced)
- P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ, where φ is the load impedance angle (power-factor angle).
- Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ; |S| = √3 V_L I_L.
- Example: 400 V line, 10 A line current, pf 0.8 lagging: P = √3 × 400 × 10 × 0.8 ≈ 5.54 kW, |S| ≈ 6.93 kVA, Q ≈ 4.16 kvar.
- Per-phase analysis: for a balanced system, solve one phase (usually as an equivalent star) and multiply power by 3.

Synchronous generators
- Construction: a rotor carrying a DC field winding (or permanent magnets) is driven by a turbine; the stator carries three windings spaced 120° electrical apart.
- The rotating field induces three EMFs in the stator; their frequency is locked to rotor speed: f = p n/120, where p is the number of poles and n the speed in rpm (equivalently f = pole pairs × revolutions per second).
- Example: on a 50 Hz grid, a 2-pole machine turns at 3000 rpm and a 4-pole machine at 1500 rpm.
- Per-phase model (resistance neglected): E = V + jX_s I, where E is the internal EMF (set by field current and speed), V the terminal voltage and X_s the synchronous reactance.
- Real power delivered to an infinite bus: P = 3 E V sin δ/X_s, with E and V per-phase values and δ the load (power) angle between E and V. More turbine torque increases δ and P; field current mainly controls reactive power.
- Synchronisation to the grid requires matching voltage magnitude, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle.

Exam tips: be explicit whether a voltage is line or phase; √3 appears in the line-phase conversion and in the line-quantity power formula; check pole count against speed and frequency.

notes.h: Binary numbers, binary arithmetic and Boolean algebra
notes.body:
Digital electronics represents information with two voltage levels, logic 0 and logic 1. This topic covers the number systems and the algebra used to describe digital circuits.

Number systems
- Binary (base 2): each bit position is a power of two. 101101₂ = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.
- Hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0–9 and A–F) groups bits in fours: 1101 0011₂ = D3₁₆. Octal groups in threes.
- Decimal to binary: repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders from last to first.
- An n-bit unsigned number ranges from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 (0–255 for 8 bits).

Signed numbers
- Two's complement is the standard: to negate, invert every bit and add 1. The most significant bit has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹.
- Range for n bits: −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 (−128 to +127 for 8 bits).
- Example: +45 = 0010 1101, invert → 1101 0010, add 1 → 1101 0011 = −45 (D3₁₆).
- Subtraction A − B is done as A + (two's complement of B), so one adder handles both.
- Overflow: adding two numbers of the same sign gives a result of the opposite sign. 100 + 50 in 8-bit two's complement gives 1001 0110, which reads as −106, because 150 exceeds +127. Sign-magnitude and one's complement have two representations of zero, which is one reason two's complement is preferred.

Boolean algebra
- Operations: AND (A·B), OR (A + B), NOT (A′ or Ā), plus XOR (A ⊕ B, true when inputs differ) and the inverted forms NAND, NOR, XNOR.
- Useful identities: A + 0 = A, A·1 = A, A + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0, A + A = A, A·A′ = 0, A + A′ = 1.
- Absorption: A + AB = A; A(A + B) = A. Also A + A′B = A + B.
- De Morgan's theorems: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′·B′.
- NAND and NOR are each universal: any logic function can be built from NAND gates alone (or NOR alone).

Canonical forms and simplification
- Sum of products (SOP): OR together the minterms (rows where output = 1). Product of sums (POS): AND together maxterms (rows where output = 0).
- Example: F = AB + AB′ + A′B. Group AB + AB′ = A(B + B′) = A, so F = A + A′B = A + B.
- Karnaugh maps arrange minterms in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ by one variable; grouping adjacent 1s in blocks of 1, 2, 4, 8 … gives a minimal SOP expression. Groups can wrap around the edges, and "don't care" entries can be used as 1s if they enlarge a group.

Exam tips: show the invert-and-add-one steps for two's complement; check the range before adding; in Boolean simplification write which law you use at each step and verify with a truth table.

A combinational circuit's outputs depend only on its present inputs (no memory). Adders and comparators are the standard examples, and they show how a truth table becomes gates.

Design procedure
1. State the inputs and outputs and write the truth table.
2. Write SOP (or POS) expressions for each output.
3. Simplify with Boolean algebra or a Karnaugh map.
4. Draw the gate-level circuit; check with a few test cases.

Half adder
Adds two bits A and B.
- Sum S = A ⊕ B; Carry C = A·B.
- Truth table: 0+0 = 00, 0+1 = 01, 1+0 = 01, 1+1 = 10 (carry, sum).

Full adder
Adds A, B and a carry-in C_in.
- S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in (1 when an odd number of inputs are 1).
- C_out = A·B + C_in·(A ⊕ B), equivalently the majority function AB + AC_in + BC_in.
- A full adder can be built from two half adders and an OR gate.

Ripple-carry adder
- Chain n full adders, feeding each C_out into the next stage's C_in; the first C_in is 0 for addition.
- Simple but slow: the worst-case delay grows linearly with n because the carry may have to ripple through every stage. Carry-lookahead adders compute carries in parallel to reduce this.
- Adder–subtractor: put an XOR gate on each B input controlled by a SUB line and also feed SUB into the first carry-in. When SUB = 1, B is inverted and 1 is added, giving A + B′ + 1 = A − B in two's complement.
- Signed overflow flag: V = C_in(MSB) ⊕ C_out(MSB).

Comparators
- Equality of single bits: E = (A ⊕ B)′ = A XNOR B. For multi-bit words, AND together the XNOR of each bit pair: A = B only if every bit matches.
- One-bit magnitude: (A > B) = A·B′ and (A < B) = A′·B.
- Multi-bit magnitude comparison works from the most significant bit down: A > B if the MSBs give A > B, or if the MSBs are equal and the next bits give A > B, and so on.
- For two 2-bit numbers A₁A₀ and B₁B₀: (A > B) = A₁B₁′ + (A₁ XNOR B₁)·A₀B₀′.

Other combinational blocks
Multiplexers (select one of several inputs), decoders (activate one of 2ⁿ outputs) and encoders are built the same way and appear alongside adders in digital design labs.

Timing note
Real gates have propagation delay; momentary wrong outputs ("glitches" or hazards) can appear while signals settle, which matters when combinational outputs drive clocked logic.

Exam tips: write the truth table first; for a full adder be ready to derive both S and C_out and draw the two-half-adder version; for comparators, explain why XNOR tests equality.

notes.h: Programming microcontrollers: the Arduino Uno and its peripherals
notes.body:
A microcontroller is a single chip containing a processor, program memory, data memory and input/output peripherals. The module uses boards such as the Arduino Uno to connect code to real circuits.

The Arduino Uno (Rev3) in brief
- Microcontroller: ATmega328P, an 8-bit AVR, clocked at 16 MHz.
- Memory: 32 KB flash for the program (a small part is used by the bootloader), 2 KB SRAM for variables, 1 KB EEPROM for non-volatile data.
- I/O: 14 digital pins (0–13), 6 of which can produce PWM (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11); 6 analogue inputs (A0–A5) feeding a 10-bit ADC.
- Operates at 5 V logic. Keep pin currents to about 20 mA; 40 mA is the absolute maximum per pin.
- Communication peripherals: UART (serial, pins 0 and 1, also via USB), SPI and I²C; hardware timers and external interrupts.

Program structure (Arduino C/C++)
- setup() runs once after reset: configure pins with pinMode(pin, OUTPUT / INPUT / INPUT_PULLUP), start Serial with Serial.begin(9600).
- loop() then runs repeatedly for ever.
- Digital I/O: digitalWrite(pin, HIGH/LOW), digitalRead(pin).
- Timing: delay(ms) blocks; millis() returns the time since start, allowing non-blocking timing (compare with a stored time instead of waiting).

Analogue input
- analogRead(pin) returns 0–1023 (10 bits). With the default 5 V reference, one step is about 5/1024 ≈ 4.9 mV, and voltage ≈ reading × 5/1024 (many tutorials use 5/1023; the difference is under 0.1 %).
- Example: a reading of 512 corresponds to about 2.5 V.
- Sensors such as thermistors or light-dependent resistors are read by placing them in a voltage divider.

"Analogue" output via PWM
- analogWrite(pin, value) with value 0–255 sets the duty cycle of a square wave (on most Uno PWM pins about 490 Hz; pins 5 and 6 about 980 Hz). It is not a true analogue voltage.
- Average voltage = duty × 5 V; analogWrite(pin, 64) gives about 25 % duty, average ≈ 1.25 V. An RC low-pass filter can smooth it into a DC level; a motor or LED averages it naturally.

Interfacing basics
- LED: a series resistor sets the current. With 5 V, a 2 V LED forward drop and 220 Ω: (5 − 2)/220 ≈ 13.6 mA.
- Push buttons need a defined idle level: use a pull-up (INPUT_PULLUP, so the pin reads LOW when pressed) or pull-down resistor; mechanical contacts bounce, so debounce in software (ignore changes for a few milliseconds) or hardware.
- Loads such as motors and relays need a transistor or driver, plus a flyback diode for inductive loads.

Exam tips: be able to write a short setup()/loop() sketch from a description, convert ADC readings to volts, compute PWM duty and series resistor values, and explain why a pull-up resistor is needed.

notes.h: Operational amplifiers: amplifiers, integrators and differentiators
notes.body:
The operational amplifier (op-amp) is a high-gain differential amplifier. Wrapped in negative feedback it becomes a precise building block whose behaviour is set by external resistors and capacitors.

The ideal op-amp
- Output V_out = A(V₊ − V₋) with open-loop gain A → ∞.
- Infinite input impedance (no current into the inputs) and zero output impedance.
- With negative feedback and the output not saturated, two "golden rules" follow: (1) V₊ = V₋ (virtual short), (2) no current flows into either input.
- The output cannot exceed the supply rails; if the formulas demand more, the op-amp saturates and the golden rules no longer hold.

Standard circuits (ideal op-amp, negative feedback)
- Inverting amplifier: input through R_in to V₋, feedback R_f from output to V₋, V₊ grounded. V₋ is a virtual earth, so V_out/V_in = −R_f/R_in. Input impedance = R_in. Example: R_f = 100 kΩ, R_in = 10 kΩ gives a gain of −10.
- Non-inverting amplifier: input to V₊, divider R_f and R₁ from output to V₋. V_out/V_in = 1 + R_f/R₁ (e.g. 11 with 100 kΩ and 10 kΩ). Very high input impedance.
- Voltage follower (buffer): output tied to V₋, gain +1. Used to stop a load from disturbing a high-impedance source.
- Summing amplifier: several inputs through resistors into the virtual earth: V_out = −R_f(V₁/R₁ + V₂/R₂ + …).
- Difference amplifier: with matched ratios, V_out = (R_f/R₁)(V₂ − V₁).

Integrator
- Replace R_f in the inverting amplifier with a capacitor C. The input current V_in/R must flow into C, so V_out(t) = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt + V_out(0).
- Example: R = 10 kΩ, C = 1 µF (RC = 10 ms) with a constant +1 V input: the output ramps at −100 V/s until it hits the negative rail.
- In the frequency domain the gain is −1/(jωRC): falls at 20 dB/decade. At DC the gain is unlimited, so input offsets cause drift; practical integrators add a large resistor in parallel with C.

Differentiator
- Swap R and C: V_out = −RC dV_in/dt; gain −jωRC rises with frequency.
- This amplifies high-frequency noise, so practical designs add a small resistor in series with C to limit high-frequency gain.

Real op-amp limits (first look)
- Finite gain-bandwidth product: closed-loop bandwidth ≈ GBW/(noise gain), e.g. a 1 MHz GBW op-amp at a non-inverting gain of 10 has about 100 kHz bandwidth.
- Slew rate limits how fast the output can change; output swing limited by the rails; input offset voltage and bias currents.

Exam tips: apply the golden rules explicitly (write the KCL at V₋); give the sign of inverting circuits; check whether the predicted output exceeds the rails; for integrators, sketch the output for a step or square-wave input.

The module ends by modelling simple control systems: a plant (the thing being controlled), a sensor that measures its output, and a controller that acts on the error. The same maths explains why op-amp circuits with feedback are so precise.

Block diagram and closed-loop gain
- Forward path G (controller × plant), feedback path H (sensor). Reference input R, output Y.
- Error signal E = R − H Y (negative feedback). Then Y = G E, so Y = G(R − HY).
- Closed-loop transfer function: T = Y/R = G/(1 + GH).
- GH is the loop gain. If GH ≫ 1, T ≈ 1/H: the output depends on the sensor, not on the plant.
- For positive feedback the denominator becomes 1 − GH, which can approach zero (instability or oscillation).

Benefits of negative feedback
- Reduced sensitivity to forward-path changes: dT/T = [1/(1 + GH)] × dG/G. Example: G = 1000, H = 0.1 gives T = 1000/101 ≈ 9.901. If G falls 10 % to 900, T = 900/91 ≈ 9.890, a change of only about 0.11 %.
- Disturbance rejection: a disturbance added at the plant output is reduced by the factor 1/(1 + GH).
- Wider bandwidth and speed of response, at the cost of lower gain (gain–bandwidth trade-off).
- The price: more components (sensor), and possible instability if the loop has too much gain at frequencies with large phase lag.

Example: op-amp as a feedback system
A non-inverting amplifier with open-loop gain A and feedback fraction β = R₁/(R₁ + R_f) has closed-loop gain A/(1 + Aβ). With A = 10⁵ and β = 0.1 it is 9.999, essentially 1/β = 10, which is why the ideal formula works.

Dynamic systems with Laplace transforms
Using the Laplace variable s (zero initial conditions):
- A first-order plant G_p(s) = K/(τs + 1) has DC gain K and time constant τ; its step response reaches 63 % of its final value at t = τ.
- With a proportional controller of gain K_p and unity feedback, the loop gain is K_pK/(τs + 1), and T(s) = K_pK/(τs + 1 + K_pK).
- Closed-loop DC gain = K_pK/(1 + K_pK) and closed-loop time constant = τ/(1 + K_pK): feedback speeds the system up.
- Steady-state error to a unit step (unity feedback, type-0 loop with DC loop gain K_L = K_pK): e_ss = 1/(1 + K_L). Example: K_L = 9 gives 10 % error and the response is 10 times faster than open loop.
- Raising gain reduces error but, in higher-order systems, eventually causes overshoot or instability; integral action removes steady-state error to a step.

Exam tips: derive T = G/(1 + GH) from the block diagram rather than quoting it; state that results assume negative feedback and a stable loop; for first-order systems give both the closed-loop gain and time constant.

questions.q: A heat engine runs between reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K. What is its endoreversible (Curzon–Ahlborn) efficiency at maximum power?
questions.why: η = 1 − √(300/600) = 1 − √0.5 ≈ 1 − 0.707 = 0.293, so about 29 %. About 50 % is the Carnot limit 1 − 300/600, which forgets the square root. About 71 % is √0.5 itself, i.e. forgetting to subtract from 1. About 25 % comes from simply halving the Carnot efficiency, which is not what the model predicts.

questions.q: A turbine's steam enters at 327 °C and the condenser is at 27 °C. What is the Carnot limit on its efficiency?
questions.why: In kelvin T_h = 600 K and T_c = 300 K, so η = 1 − 300/600 = 0.5, about 50 %. About 92 % comes from using Celsius directly (1 − 27/327). About 8 % is the ratio 27/327 in Celsius, i.e. both the wrong units and forgetting to subtract from 1. About 45 % is 1 − 327/600, which mixes a Celsius temperature with a kelvin one.

questions.q: A gas-fired plant has turbine inlet temperature 1500 K and rejects heat at 300 K. (a) Find the Carnot efficiency. (b) Find the endoreversible efficiency at maximum power. (c) Explain briefly why real plants operate nearer (b) than (a).
markScheme: Carnot needs reversible heat transfer, so infinitely slow operation and zero power
Real plants must deliver useful power, so finite temperature differences for heat transfer are unavoidable
questions.modelAnswer: (a) η_C = 1 − 300/1500 = 0.80. (b) η_CA = 1 − √(300/1500) = 1 − 0.447 = 0.553, about 55 %. (c) The Carnot efficiency is only reached by a reversible engine whose heat transfers happen across infinitesimal temperature differences, which take infinite time, so its power output is zero. A plant must deliver power, so heat has to cross finite temperature drops; the endoreversible model captures this and maximising power gives an efficiency close to (b).

questions.q: A 12 V source in series with 4 kΩ drives a 12 kΩ resistor to ground; the output is across the 12 kΩ. What is the Thévenin equivalent at the output?
questions.why: V_Th is the divider output 12 × 12/16 = 9 V and R_Th is 4 kΩ in parallel with 12 kΩ = 3 kΩ. 12 V in series with 16 kΩ ignores the divider and adds the resistors in series. 9 V with 16 kΩ gets V_Th right but treats the resistors as in series when the source is shorted, when in fact they are in parallel. 3 V uses the drop across the 4 kΩ resistor (12 × 4/16) instead of the output voltage.

questions.q: Three currents flow into a node: 2 A, −0.5 A and I₃. A single current of 4 A leaves the node. What is I₃?
questions.why: KCL: total in = total out, so 2 + (−0.5) + I₃ = 4, giving I₃ = 2.5 A. 1.5 A comes from treating the −0.5 A as +0.5 A (2 + 0.5 + I₃ = 4). 5.5 A comes from moving the known inflows to the wrong side of the balance, adding them to the 4 A outflow instead of subtracting (I₃ = 4 + 2 + (−0.5)). −2.5 A results from treating I₃ as a current leaving the node (2 − 0.5 − I₃ = 4), which flips its sign.

questions.q: For the network of 12 V, 4 kΩ series and 12 kΩ shunt (output across 12 kΩ): (a) find the Norton equivalent; (b) find the load voltage and current for a 6 kΩ load; (c) explain why the load voltage is less than the open-circuit voltage.
markScheme: Load current = 9 V/(3 k + 6 k) = 1 mA
Explanation: drop across internal R_Th (loading) reduces terminal voltage
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Shorting the output removes the 12 kΩ path, so I_N = 12 V/4 kΩ = 3 mA, in parallel with R_N = 4 k ∥ 12 k = 3 kΩ. (b) Using the Thévenin form (V_Th = I_N R_N = 9 V), I = 9/(3 + 6) kΩ = 1 mA and V = 1 mA × 6 kΩ = 6 V. (c) The load current flows through the equivalent internal resistance of 3 kΩ, dropping 3 V, so only 6 V of the 9 V open-circuit voltage appears across the load.

questions.q: A source has V_Th = 9 V and R_Th = 3 kΩ. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a resistive load?
questions.why: Maximum power occurs at R_L = R_Th: P = V_Th²/(4R_Th) = 81/12000 = 6.75 mW. 27 mW is V_Th²/R_Th, the power dissipated inside R_Th when the output is short-circuited, not power delivered to a load. 13.5 mW is V_Th²/(2R_Th), dividing by 2 instead of 4. 3 mW confuses power with the short-circuit current of 3 mA.

questions.q: The impedance of a 1 µF capacitor at 1 kHz is closest to:
questions.why: Z_C = −j/(ωC) = −j/(2π × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ −j159 Ω. −j1000 Ω uses 1/(fC) and forgets the 2π. −j6.28 mΩ is ωC itself, i.e. inverting the formula. +j159 Ω has the right magnitude but the sign of an inductor's reactance.

questions.q: A source has Thévenin impedance Z_Th = 4 + j3 Ω and open-circuit voltage 8 V rms. (a) What load gives maximum power and how much power is that? (b) If the load must be a pure resistor, what value maximises power and how much power is delivered?
markScheme: For a purely resistive load, optimum R_L = |Z_Th| = 5 Ω
Power = 0.843² × 5 ≈ 3.56 W, less than the conjugate-matched 4 W
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The conjugate match Z_L = 4 − j3 Ω cancels the reactance, leaving 8 Ω total, so I = 1 A rms and P = I²R_L = 4 W (equivalently 64/(4 × 4)). (b) With a resistor only, the optimum is R_L = |Z_Th| = 5 Ω. The total impedance is 9 + j3 Ω, magnitude 9.49 Ω, so I ≈ 0.843 A rms and P ≈ 0.843² × 5 ≈ 3.56 W, less than 4 W because the source reactance is not cancelled.

questions.q: A 10 V rms source at ω = 2000 rad/s drives 100 Ω in series with 50 mH. What is the current phasor?
questions.why: X_L = ωL = 100 Ω, so Z = 100 + j100 = 141.4∠45° Ω and I = 10∠0°/141.4∠45° = 0.0707∠−45° A: current lags in an inductive circuit. 0.1∠0° A ignores the inductor. 0.0707∠+45° A has the right magnitude but the sign of the angle flipped, which would mean a capacitive circuit. 0.05∠−45° A comes from adding R and X_L as plain numbers (200 Ω) rather than as perpendicular components.

questions.q: Using rms phasors, V = 230∠0° V and I = 10∠−30° A. What is the real power absorbed?
questions.why: S = V I* = 230 × 10∠30° = 2300∠30° VA, so P = 2300 cos 30° ≈ 1992 W (Q ≈ 1150 var). 2300 W is the apparent power, ignoring the power factor. 1150 W is 2300 sin 30°, the reactive power, so sine and cosine have been swapped. 1328 W divides 2300 by √3, a three-phase factor that does not belong in a single-phase calculation.

questions.q: Express i(t) = 5 cos(100t − 60°) A and v(t) = 20 sin(100t) V as peak-value phasors (cosine reference) and find the impedance Z = V/I in rectangular form.
questions.modelAnswer: I = 5∠−60° A. Since sin x = cos(x − 90°), V = 20∠−90° V. Then Z = V/I = (20/5)∠(−90° + 60°) = 4∠−30° Ω = 3.46 − j2.00 Ω. The negative imaginary part shows the load is capacitive (current leads voltage by 30°).

questions.q: A series RLC circuit has L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF and R = 10 Ω. What is its −3 dB bandwidth?
questions.why: B = f₀/Q = R/(2πL) = 10/(2π × 0.01) ≈ 159 Hz (f₀ ≈ 5.03 kHz, Q ≈ 31.6). About 1 kHz is R/L = 1000 rad/s read as hertz, i.e. forgetting to divide by 2π. About 5.0 kHz is the resonant frequency itself, not the bandwidth. About 31.6 Hz is the numerical value of Q, which is dimensionless and not a frequency.

questions.q: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Its cut-off frequency is closest to:
questions.why: f_c = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴ s) ≈ 1.59 kHz. 10 kHz is 1/(RC) = 10⁴ rad/s quoted as hertz, missing the 2π. 62.8 kHz multiplies 1/(RC) by 2π instead of dividing by it. 159 kHz comes from mis-converting 100 nF as 1 nF.

questions.q: Derive the transfer function of a first-order RC high-pass filter (output across R) and show that at ω = 1/(RC) its gain is −3 dB and its phase is +45°.
markScheme: Multiply through by jωC: H = jωRC/(1 + jωRC)
questions.modelAnswer: With output across R, H = R/(R + 1/(jωC)). Multiplying numerator and denominator by jωC gives H = jωRC/(1 + jωRC). At ω = 1/(RC), H = j/(1 + j). |j| = 1 and |1 + j| = √2, so |H| = 1/√2 and the gain is 20 log₁₀(0.707) ≈ −3.0 dB. The angle is ∠j − ∠(1 + j) = 90° − 45° = +45°, so the output leads the input.

questions.q: A balanced star-connected load draws 10 A from a 400 V (line) three-phase supply at 0.8 power factor. What real power does it take?
questions.why: P = √3 × 400 × 10 × 0.8 ≈ 5.54 kW. 9.6 kW is 3 × 400 × 10 × 0.8, using line voltage where the formula with a factor 3 needs phase voltage. 3.2 kW is 400 × 10 × 0.8, a single-phase calculation that misses the √3. 6.93 kW is the apparent power √3 × 400 × 10, ignoring the power factor.

questions.q: A synchronous generator connected to a 50 Hz grid runs at 1500 rpm. How many poles does it have?
questions.why: From f = p n/120, p = 120 × 50/1500 = 4 poles. 2 comes from using f = p n/60, which gives pole pairs, and reporting that as the number of poles (a 2-pole machine would need 3000 rpm). 3 confuses the number of phases with the number of poles. 30 divides the speed in rpm by the frequency without converting rpm to revolutions per second.

questions.q: A 400 V (line), 50 Hz, star-connected balanced load has impedance 20∠36.87° Ω per phase. Find the phase voltage, line current, power factor and total real power.
questions.modelAnswer: Phase voltage = 400/√3 ≈ 230.9 V. In star the line current equals the phase current: 230.9/20 ≈ 11.55 A, lagging the phase voltage by 36.87°, so pf = 0.8 lagging. Total power P = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ = 3 × 230.9 × 11.55 × 0.8 ≈ 6.40 kW, the same as √3 V_L I_L cos φ.

questions.q: What is −45 in 8-bit two's complement?
questions.why: +45 is 0010 1101; inverting gives 1101 0010 and adding 1 gives 1101 0011. 1010 1101 is sign-magnitude (sign bit set on +45). 1101 0010 is the one's complement, the step before adding 1. 0010 1101 is +45 itself.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to F = AB + AB′ + A′B?
questions.why: AB + AB′ = A, then A + A′B = A + B. The XOR expression A ⊕ B fails because F is 1 when A = B = 1 (the AB term), but XOR is 0 there. AB is only one of the three terms. A drops the A′B term, so it misses the row A = 0, B = 1 where F = 1.

questions.q: Add 0110 0100 and 0011 0010 as 8-bit two's complement numbers. Give the binary result, its decimal interpretation, and explain whether overflow has occurred.
markScheme: Overflow: two positive operands give a negative result; true sum 150 exceeds +127
questions.modelAnswer: 0110 0100 = +100 and 0011 0010 = +50. Their binary sum is 1001 0110. With the MSB weighted −128, this reads −128 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −106. Overflow has occurred: two positive numbers produced a negative result because the true sum, 150, is outside the 8-bit range of −128 to +127.

questions.q: For a full adder with A = 1, B = 1 and C_in = 1, what are S and C_out?
questions.why: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = binary 11, so S = 1 and C_out = 1 (S = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 1 = 1; majority of three 1s is 1). S = 0, C_out = 1 is the half-adder result for 1 + 1, forgetting the carry-in. S = 1, C_out = 0 drops the carry entirely. S = 0, C_out = 0 treats the XOR of three 1s as 0 and ignores the majority carry.

questions.q: Which gate, applied to one bit of A and the matching bit of B, outputs 1 exactly when the two bits are equal?
questions.why: XNOR outputs 1 when its inputs are the same (00 or 11). XOR does the opposite, giving 1 when they differ. AND gives 1 only for 11, missing the 00 case. NAND gives 1 for 00, 01 and 10, so it is 1 for unequal inputs too.

questions.q: Starting from the truth table, derive minimal expressions for the sum and carry outputs of a full adder, and show how it can be built from two half adders and one OR gate.
markScheme: Correct 8-row truth table for A, B, C_in → S, C_out
S is 1 for an odd number of 1s: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in
C_out = AB + AC_in + BC_in, or AB + C_in(A ⊕ B)
First half adder gives P = A ⊕ B and G = AB; second adds P and C_in giving S = P ⊕ C_in and C_in·P
C_out = G + C_in·P using an OR gate
questions.modelAnswer: The truth table has S = 1 in rows 001, 010, 100 and 111 (odd number of 1s), so S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in. C_out = 1 in rows 011, 101, 110 and 111, which a K-map groups as AB + AC_in + BC_in; this equals AB + C_in(A ⊕ B). Build: half adder 1 takes A, B and gives P = A ⊕ B and G = AB. Half adder 2 takes P and C_in and gives S = P ⊕ C_in and a carry C_in·P. An OR gate combines the two carries: C_out = AB + C_in(A ⊕ B).

questions.q: On an Arduino Uno with the default 5 V reference, analogRead returns 205. The input voltage is closest to:

questions.q: analogWrite(9, 191) on an Uno produces a PWM signal on pin 9. What is its average voltage, assuming 5 V logic?
questions.why: Duty = 191/255 ≈ 0.749, so the average is about 0.749 × 5 ≈ 3.75 V. About 0.93 V is 191/1023 × 5, using the 10-bit ADC range instead of the 8-bit PWM range. About 1.25 V is the off-time fraction (64/255 × 5), i.e. the inverted duty. About 2.47 V uses the right duty cycle but a 3.3 V logic level; the Uno runs at 5 V.

questions.q: Write an Arduino sketch outline that reads a potentiometer on A0 and sets the brightness of an LED on pin 9 in proportion, and choose a series resistor for the LED (forward voltage 2 V, target 10 mA, 5 V supply).
markScheme: setup(): pinMode(9, OUTPUT) (analogue input needs no pinMode)
Scale to 0–255, e.g. v/4 or map(v, 0, 1023, 0, 255), then analogWrite(9, value)
Resistor R = (5 − 2)/0.010 = 300 Ω; choose nearest standard value such as 330 Ω
Notes that analogWrite gives PWM, and pin 9 is a PWM pin
questions.modelAnswer: void setup() { pinMode(9, OUTPUT); }  void loop() { int v = analogRead(A0); analogWrite(9, v / 4); }  analogRead gives 0–1023 and analogWrite expects 0–255, so dividing by 4 (or using map) rescales it. Pin 9 supports PWM, so the LED's average current, and its apparent brightness, follow the duty cycle. Resistor: R = (5 − 2)/0.010 = 300 Ω; the next standard value, 330 Ω, gives about 9 mA, safely inside the pin rating.

questions.q: A non-inverting amplifier has R_f = 100 kΩ and R₁ = 10 kΩ. What is its gain?
questions.why: Non-inverting gain = 1 + R_f/R₁ = 1 + 10 = 11. −10 is the inverting-amplifier formula −R_f/R_in. 10 forgets the '1 +' term. 0.09 is R₁/(R₁ + R_f), the feedback fraction β, not the gain (the gain is approximately 1/β = 11).

questions.q: An ideal integrator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF, starting from 0 V. A constant +0.5 V is applied for 2 ms. What is the output at the end (rails ±15 V)?
questions.why: RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁷ = 1 ms. V_out = −(1/RC) × 0.5 V × 2 ms = −1 V. +1 V misses the inversion of the inverting integrator. −0.1 V comes from using RC = 10 ms (taking C as 1 µF). −0.25 V inverts the time ratio, multiplying 0.5 V by RC/t = 1 ms/2 ms instead of t/RC.

questions.q: Using the ideal op-amp rules, derive the gain of an inverting amplifier with input resistor R_in and feedback resistor R_f, and state its input impedance.
markScheme: V₊ grounded so V₋ = 0 (virtual earth) by negative feedback
No current into V₋, so the same I flows through R_f
Input impedance = R_in (source sees R_in to virtual earth)
questions.modelAnswer: With negative feedback, V₋ = V₊ = 0 V (a virtual earth). The current through R_in is V_in/R_in. Because no current enters the op-amp input, all of it flows through R_f, so V_out = 0 − (V_in/R_in)R_f, giving V_out/V_in = −R_f/R_in. The source drives R_in into a point held at 0 V, so the input impedance is R_in.

questions.q: A system has forward gain G = 1000 and feedback gain H = 0.1. If G drops by 10 %, by roughly how much does the closed-loop gain change?
questions.why: T = 1000/101 ≈ 9.901 and with G = 900, T = 900/91 ≈ 9.890, a change of about 0.11 % (consistent with 10 %/(1 + GH) = 10 %/101 ≈ 0.1 %). 10 % is the open-loop change, ignoring feedback. 1.1 % compares the new gain 9.890 with the ideal value 1/H = 10 instead of with the original closed-loop gain 9.901. 0.01 % divides by 1000 instead of 101, using G alone instead of the loop gain.

questions.q: A first-order plant K/(τs + 1) with K = 2 and τ = 0.5 s is placed under proportional control K_p = 4 with unity feedback. What is the closed-loop time constant?
questions.why: Loop gain K_pK = 8, so the closed-loop time constant is τ/(1 + 8) = 0.5/9 ≈ 0.0556 s. 0.5 s is the open-loop time constant. 0.0625 s divides by 8 rather than 1 + 8. 4.5 s multiplies by (1 + K_pK) instead of dividing, which would make feedback slow the system down.

questions.q: Derive the closed-loop transfer function of a single-loop negative feedback system with forward path G and feedback path H, and use it to explain why a high loop gain makes the closed-loop gain insensitive to G.
markScheme: E = R − HY and Y = GE
Y = G(R − HY) → Y(1 + GH) = GR
For GH ≫ 1, T ≈ 1/H, independent of G
questions.modelAnswer: The error is E = R − HY and the output is Y = GE, so Y = GR − GHY, giving Y(1 + GH) = GR and T = Y/R = G/(1 + GH). Differentiating, dT/dG = 1/(1 + GH)², so (dT/T)/(dG/G) = 1/(1 + GH). When the loop gain GH is large this ratio is small, and T tends to 1/H, which depends only on the feedback element (e.g. precise resistors), not on the uncertain forward gain.

questions.q:
A 24 V DC source with internal resistance 6 Ω feeds a node P. A 3 Ω resistor connects P to ground, and a 2 Ω resistor connects P to output terminal X; the load is connected between X and ground.
(a) Find the Thévenin and Norton equivalents seen by the load. [6]
(b) Find the load resistance for maximum power transfer and the maximum power. [4]
(c) Find the load power and the source-to-load efficiency for R_L = 12 Ω and comment. [5]
(d) At a particular frequency the source network has Thévenin impedance 4 + j3 Ω and open-circuit voltage 8 V rms. Find the power delivered to a conjugate-matched load and to the best purely resistive load. [5]
markScheme: (c) Efficiency relative to the Thévenin source: 12/16 = 75 %, higher than the 50 % at matching
(d) Conjugate load 4 − j3 Ω: P = 64/16 = 4 W
Clear statement of methods and units throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Open-circuit: no current flows in the 2 Ω resistor, so V_X = V_P = 24 × 3/(6 + 3) = 8 V. Turning the source off (short circuit), the resistance seen from X is 2 + (6 ∥ 3) = 2 + 18/9 = 4 Ω. So the Thévenin equivalent is 8 V in series with 4 Ω, and the Norton equivalent is I_N = 8/4 = 2 A in parallel with 4 Ω. (Check: shorting X, 6 Ω in series with 3 ∥ 2 = 1.2 Ω draws 24/7.2 = 3.33 A; the divider sends 3.33 × 3/5 = 2 A through the 2 Ω branch.)

(b) For a resistive load, maximum power is at R_L = R_Th = 4 Ω: P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th) = 64/16 = 4 W, with 1 A flowing.

(c) With 12 Ω: I = 8/(4 + 12) = 0.5 A and P_L = 0.25 × 12 = 3 W. The efficiency relative to the Thévenin equivalent is R_L/(R_L + R_Th) = 12/16 = 75 %, against 50 % at the matched point. Less power reaches the load, but a much larger share of the power drawn is used usefully, which is why power systems avoid matching. (Note the Thévenin equivalent gives correct terminal behaviour but not the real internal losses of the original network.)

(d) Conjugate match: Z_L = 4 − j3 Ω, total 8 Ω, I = 1 A rms, P = 1² × 4 = 4 W. If the load must be resistive, the best value is R_L = |Z_Th| = 5 Ω; the total impedance is 9 + j3 Ω with magnitude 9.49 Ω, I = 8/9.49 ≈ 0.843 A rms and P ≈ 0.843² × 5 ≈ 3.56 W. The uncancelled source reactance costs about 11 % of the available power.

questions.q:
(a) An op-amp with finite open-loop gain A is used as a non-inverting amplifier with R_f = 90 kΩ and R₁ = 10 kΩ. Model it as a negative feedback loop and derive its closed-loop gain in terms of A and β. Evaluate it for A = 10⁵ and for A = 5 × 10⁴, and comment. [8]
(b) An ideal inverting integrator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF and starts at 0 V. Its input is +0.5 V for 0 ≤ t < 2 ms and then −0.5 V for 2 ≤ t < 4 ms. Sketch and dimension the output, given ±15 V rails. [7]
(c) Explain why practical integrators and differentiators need extra components. [5]
markScheme: (a) β = R₁/(R₁ + R_f) = 0.1; V₋ = βV_out; V_out = A(V_in − βV_out)
(a) A = 10⁵: 9.9990; A = 5 × 10⁴: 9.9980; halving A changes the gain by only about 0.01 %
(b) RC = 1 ms; slope −V_in/RC = −500 V/s during the first 2 ms
(b) Output ramps linearly from 0 to −1 V at 2 ms, then back up to 0 V at 4 ms (triangular), well inside the rails
(c) Integrator: infinite DC gain integrates offset/bias, drifting to a rail; add a resistor across C
(c) Differentiator: gain rising with frequency amplifies noise and can be unstable; add a series resistor with C (and/or small capacitor across R_f)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The feedback network is a divider, so V₋ = βV_out with β = R₁/(R₁ + R_f) = 10/100 = 0.1. The op-amp gives V_out = A(V_in − βV_out), so V_out(1 + Aβ) = AV_in and the closed-loop gain is A/(1 + Aβ). This is the standard feedback result with G = A and H = β. For A = 10⁵: 10⁵/(1 + 10⁴) = 9.9990. For A = 5 × 10⁴: 5 × 10⁴/(1 + 5000) = 9.9980. Halving the open-loop gain changes the closed-loop gain by only about 0.01 %, and both are close to the ideal 1/β = 1 + R_f/R₁ = 10, showing why feedback makes the gain depend on the resistors rather than on A.

(b) RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁷ = 1 ms. For an ideal inverting integrator dV_out/dt = −V_in/RC. During 0–2 ms, V_in = +0.5 V, so the output falls at 500 V/s, reaching −0.5 × 2/1 = −1 V at t = 2 ms. During 2–4 ms, V_in = −0.5 V, so the output rises at 500 V/s back to 0 V at 4 ms. The output is a triangle between 0 and −1 V, comfortably within ±15 V, so the ideal analysis holds.

(c) An ideal integrator has gain −1/(jωRC), which is infinite at DC. Any input offset voltage or bias current is integrated, so the output drifts until it saturates; a large resistor across C limits the DC gain (making a 'lossy' integrator that integrates only above a corner frequency). An ideal differentiator has gain magnitude ωRC that rises without limit, so high-frequency noise is strongly amplified, and the op-amp's own phase lag can make it ring or oscillate; a resistor in series with the input capacitor (and often a small capacitor across the feedback resistor) caps the high-frequency gain.
